_source: Hand-maintained facts about which kinds of contest each state puts on its November general-election ballot, and in which years: every state's legislative election calendar (NCSL, 'State Legislative Elections'; Ballotpedia, 'State legislative elections, 2026'), and its judicial selection method (National Center for State Courts, 'Methods of Judicial Selection', judicialselection.us; Ballotpedia, 'Judicial selection in the states'), each checked against the state constitution where `_why` cites it. Not calculated values (AGENTS.md 3a): change an entry when a state changes its law, citing the change.
_method: Read by app/state_ballot_scope.py for the state ballot page's `omits` list (api/elections.state_ballot), which must name only gaps that exist: a state that elects no judges, holds no retention votes, or has no legislative election in a year must not be told its page omits them. Each kind is a cycle {"every": N, "from": YEAR} — on the November general ballot in YEAR and every N years after (and before) — or null: never on a November general ballot. Judicial contests count every level the state elects in November (trial courts included); retention means a yes/no vote on keeping a sitting judge.

AL._why: Both chambers serve four-year terms elected together in gubernatorial years (Ala. Const. art. IV).

AZ._why: Merit-selected appellate and large-county judges stand for retention; superior court judges in smaller counties are elected (Ariz. Const. art. VI, §§12, 37-38).

AR._why: Nonpartisan judicial elections are held with the March primary; a judgeship with no majority winner goes to a runoff at the November general.

CA._why: Supreme Court and appellate justices stand for retention at the gubernatorial general election (Cal. Const. art. VI, §16(a)); superior court contests left undecided in June go to November.

CT._why: Supreme, Appellate and Superior Court judges are nominated by the Governor and appointed by the General Assembly (Conn. Const. art. V, §2); probate judges are elected to four-year terms (2022, 2026).

DE._why: Judges are appointed by the Governor with Senate confirmation (Del. Const. art. IV, §3).

DC._why: The District has no state legislature; the Council of the District of Columbia's seats are elected in even years. Judges are appointed by the President (D.C. Code §11-1501).

FL._why: Appellate judges stand for retention (Fla. Const. art. V, §10); circuit and county contests undecided in August go to November.

HI._why: Judges are appointed by the Governor or Chief Justice and retained by the Judicial Selection Commission, not by voters (Haw. Const. art. VI, §3).

ID._why: Nonpartisan judicial elections are held in May; a seat with no majority winner goes to the November general.

IL._why: Judges are first elected in partisan contests and then retained (Ill. Const. art. VI, §12).

KS._why: Appellate and most district judges stand for retention; district judges in the other judicial districts are elected in partisan contests (Kan. Const. art. 3, §§5-6).

LA._why: The Legislature is elected every four years in odd years (2023, 2027).

ME._why: State court judges are nominated by the Governor and confirmed by the Legislature (Me. Const. art. V, pt. 1, §8); county probate judges are elected to four-year terms (2022, 2026).

MD._why: Both chambers serve four-year terms elected together in gubernatorial years (Md. Const. art. III, §6).

MA._why: Judges are appointed by the Governor with the Governor's Council's consent and serve to age 70 (Mass. Const. pt. 2, ch. II, §1, art. IX; amend. art. XCVIII).

MS._why: The Legislature is elected every four years in odd years (2023, 2027).

MO._why: Appellate and plan-circuit judges stand for retention; judges in the other circuits are elected in partisan contests (Mo. Const. art. V, §25(a)-(c)).

MT._why: Judges are elected in nonpartisan contests; an incumbent running unopposed stands for retention instead (Mont. Const. art. VII, §8(2)).

NH._why: Judges are nominated by the Governor and confirmed by the Executive Council, serving to age 70 (N.H. Const. pt. II, arts. 46, 78).

NJ._why: The Legislature is elected in odd years (N.J. Const. art. IV, §2). Judges are appointed by the Governor with Senate consent (N.J. Const. art. VI, §6).

NM._why: Judges are first elected in partisan contests and then retained (N.M. Const. art. VI, §33).

NY._why: Supreme Court and county court judges are elected in partisan contests every November.

OH._why: Appellate and common pleas judges are elected in even years, municipal and county court judges in odd years.

OK._why: Appellate judges stand for retention (Okla. Const. art. VII-B, §2); district judges are elected in nonpartisan contests, with runoffs in November.

PA._why: Judges are elected, and retained, at the municipal election, held in odd years (Pa. Const. art. V, §§13(a), 15(b); art. VII, §3).

RI._why: Judges are nominated by the Governor from a Judicial Nominating Commission list and serve for life (R.I. Const. art. X, §4).

SC._why: Judges are elected by the General Assembly, not by voters (S.C. Const. art. V, §§3, 8).

SD._why: Supreme Court justices stand for retention; circuit judges are elected in nonpartisan contests (S.D. Const. art. V, §§7, 9).

TN._why: Judicial elections, retention votes included, are held at the August election, not in November (Tenn. Const. art. VII, §5).

VT._why: Probate judges and assistant judges are elected to four-year terms (2022, 2026); Supreme and Superior Court judges are retained by the General Assembly, not by voters.

VA._why: The General Assembly is elected in odd years (Va. Const. art. IV, §§2-3) and elects the judges (Va. Const. art. VI, §7).

WV._why: Judges are elected in nonpartisan contests decided at the May primary election, not in November (W. Va. Code §3-5-6a).

WI._why: Judges are elected at the April spring election, not in November (Wis. Const. art. VII, §§4, 5, 7, 9).
